titre: The 74-Minute CD and the Beethoven Myth
accroche: They say Beethoven's Ninth set the length of the CD. The engineer who designed its recording code recalls a different chronology
contenu_vulgarise:
According to the official story published by Philips, which engineer Kees Schouhamer Immink cites, the length of the CD was “determined posthumously by Beethoven.” Sony supposedly wanted the Ninth Symphony to fit on a single disc: Sony's website, Immink reports, explains that it was the favorite piece of the wife of Norio Ohga, the group's vice president. Philips supposedly checked with its subsidiary PolyGram. Karajan's Ninth with the Berlin Philharmonic runs 66 minutes, but the longest known performance, a mono recording by Wilhelm Furtwängler at the Bayreuth Festival in 1951, runs 74. Hence, the story goes, the 74 minutes, and a diameter of 120 millimeters to hold them.

## What the minutes say

Immink took part in the meetings of the Philips-Sony committee. He reread the minutes. On December 20, 1979, in Tokyo, each partner notes the parameters it prefers: Philips proposes a 115-millimeter disc, the size of a compact cassette, Sony a 100-millimeter one, with sixty minutes in both cases. In May 1980, in Eindhoven, the minutes record a diameter of 120 millimeters and a length of 75 minutes. No record explains the change.

At that point, the channel code, the way data is written onto the disc and therefore its density, has not been chosen. Immink is working on a new code, EFM (eight-to-fourteen modulation), 30% denser than Philips's M3 code. Sony first rejects it, then accepts it on June 19, 1980, in Tokyo. That density could have been used to shrink the disc to 115, even 100 millimeters, while keeping 74 minutes and 33 seconds, or to raise the length to 97 minutes. Immink writes that changing the diameter was not considered politically feasible, the executives having decided on 120 millimeters, and that the 97-minute length was not even considered. The density was lowered by 30% to widen manufacturing margins. Wikipedia sums up that Immink calls the story a myth.

## The factory's part

Immink judges the real story less romantic than the public-relations account. PolyGram, a Philips subsidiary, had set up a plant in Hanover capable of producing 115-millimeter discs in large quantities. Sony had no comparable facility. With a 115-millimeter standard, Philips would have gained a clear commercial advantage. Sony knew it and did not want that balance of power. Immink writes that the result is known, without saying in so many words that this rivalry fixed the 120 millimeters. Wikipedia adds that commercial disputes also played a role.

## The shift

Herbert von Karajan was, according to Wikipedia, an ambassador for the format as early as 1979. The first test disc, pressed in December 1980, is not the Ninth but Strauss's *An Alpine Symphony*, by the Berlin Philharmonic he conducts.

The disc holds 74 minutes and 33 seconds at most. In practice, Immink writes, the ceiling was 72 minutes, the length of the U-Matic video recorder. Furtwängler's Ninth therefore could fit entirely on a single CD only in 1988, six years after launch.

repere.texte: On June 19, 1980, Sony accepts in Tokyo the EFM code, 30% denser than Philips's. The 120-millimeter diameter and the 75-minute length were already in the May 1980 minutes.
repere.source: K. A. Schouhamer Immink, “Shannon, Beethoven, and the Compact Disc,” IEEE Information Theory Society Newsletter, December 2007, pp. 42-46

carte.punch: Beethoven's Ninth does not by itself explain the CD's diameter, according to engineer Immink.
carte.idee: They say Beethoven's Ninth set the length of the CD. The minutes reread by Kees Immink, the project's engineer, record a 120 mm diameter in May 1980, before the recording code was chosen in June, with a factory rivalry in the background.

quiz.question: According to Kees Immink, what fact contradicts the idea that the CD's diameter follows from the length of the Ninth?
choix: No recording of the Ninth lasted 74 minutes, the longest running 66
As early as December 1979, Philips and Sony had both chosen a 120 mm diameter
The 120 mm diameter is recorded in the May 1980 minutes, before the density code was chosen
The EFM code, chosen as early as 1979, already required a 120 mm disc to reach 74 minutes
quiz.explication: The minutes reread by Immink record 120 mm and 75 minutes in May 1980, while the channel code is only accepted on June 19, 1980; in December 1979, Philips preferred 115 mm and Sony 100 mm. The longest known Ninth runs 74 minutes (Furtwängler, 1951), contrary to the first answer. And EFM, 30% denser, would have made it possible to fit 74 minutes on 115 or 100 mm: it did not force the 120 mm.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What length does Philips propose at the December 20, 1979 meeting in Tokyo?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On December 20, 1979, in Tokyo, Philips proposes a 115-millimeter disc, the size of a compact cassette, for sixty minutes, while Sony proposed 100 millimeters.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Immink, what was the practical ceiling on a CD's length, before the format fully caught on?
choix: 72 minutes, the length of the U-Matic video recorder
60 minutes, the length of a cassette
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Immink writes that in practice the ceiling was 72 minutes, the length of the U-Matic video recorder used for recording, although in theory the disc could hold 74 minutes and 33 seconds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which disc is pressed first as a test of the format, in December 1980?
choix: Strauss's An Alpine Symphony, by the Berlin Philharmonic
Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, by I Musici
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first test disc, pressed in December 1980, is not the Ninth but Strauss's An Alpine Symphony, by the Berlin Philharmonic that Karajan conducts.
